title: How a model sees
description: Models understand more than text: photos and video become tokens too. Show the model a short clip — and see what it notices.

steps.text: So far we've talked to the model in words. But modern models understand pictures and video too. Meta's Muse Spark, for example, watches a short clip the same way it reads text.

steps.definition: The model understands more than one kind of data: text, images, sound, video. Inside, all of it turns into tokens — the model's common language.
steps.example: You send a photo of a receipt — and the model reads the total just as it would in text.

steps.text: A model doesn't watch video “like a movie.” The clip is split into frames, the frames into small image patches, and all of that becomes tokens. That's why a long video means lots of tokens: slower and more expensive than a short one.

steps.caption: Pick a frame rate and see what the model manages to catch. Tokens per frame are just an example: every model has its own price

steps.instruction: Let's try it for real. Tap “Show an example” — I'll send the model six seconds of someone's desk and show you what it saw. Or film your own: 5–10 seconds of a desk, a shelf or the view from a window.
steps.videoPrompt: You are a friendly teacher in a lesson about how AI models see. The learner sent a short video: a clip of their own surroundings or a sample clip of a desk. 1) List the main things you see, roughly in the order they appear. 2) Name one detail you are not sure about and say why: blur, angle, lighting or speed. 3) In two sentences, explain how you got this from the video: you look at separate frames, so fast or tiny things can slip between them. Keep it warm and short, under 120 words.

steps.text: Look at the answer: the model named the objects but was unsure about something. That's expected. It sees separate frames, not continuous motion, so anything fast, tiny or dark easily slips past.

steps.question: Why might the model miss that you lifted a cup for a split second?
steps.answer: It doesn't watch continuous video — it looks at separate frames. If the movement fit between two frames, for the model it never happened.

steps.instruction: Now let's see it differently. Muse Spark describes what it saw in words, while Meta's SAM 3.1 can point: you name one thing and the model finds every one of them in the photo. Tap “Show an example” (a desk with a laptop, a cup, a plant and a cat) or use your own photo. Name one thing in English: cup, laptop, plant, cat.

steps.text: Now about privacy. The video goes to the model provider in full — with everything in the frame. So keep documents, screens with passwords and people who haven't agreed out of the shot. A clip filmed here is deleted by the app right after the analysis.

In short. A model understands more than text: pictures and video turn into tokens too. Video is frames, and anything fast or small can easily slip between them. A longer clip means more tokens — slower and more expensive. And everything in the frame goes to the provider.

questions.q: What does the model turn a video into before it “watches” it?
options: Frames, and the frames into tokens
A description written by a person
questions.explain: The clip is split into frames, and the frames become tokens — like words in a text.

questions.q: Why does a long video cost more than a short one?
options: The provider charges by the minute
Video is always ten times pricier
questions.explain: Every frame is tokens, and tokens are what you pay for.

questions.q: What should you check before sending a video to a model?
options: That the clip was shot in 4K
That the video is over a minute long
That nothing private is in the frame
questions.explain: The video goes to the provider in full — with everything in the frame.
